Gladys Aylward
GLAD-iss AYL-werd
proper noun
Gladys from a Welsh name long linked with gladness; Aylward, an Old English surname meaning “noble guardian.”

📖 Biblical Definition

Gladys Aylward (1902–1970) was an English parlour-maid whom no mission board would accept, yet who spent her own meagre savings on a one-way rail ticket across Siberia to reach China in 1932. Rejected as unqualified, she went anyway, convinced that the Lord who calls also equips. She settled at Yangcheng, opened with an older missionary the Inn of the Eighth Happiness, and there told gospel stories to muleteers passing through the mountains. She learned the language, was appointed a government foot-inspector to end the binding of girls’ feet, and used the office to preach Christ in every village she entered. When the Japanese invasion swept the province, Aylward led roughly a hundred orphaned children on a desperate trek over the mountains and across the Yellow River to safety, half-starved and footsore, singing as they went. Her life is a standing rebuke to the notion that God only uses the credentialed and the strong. She was small, poor, and unschooled, and the Lord made her a deliverer of children and a herald of the cross. Becoming a Chinese citizen, she gave her whole life to a people not her own. Her courage flowed not from temperament but from faith in a sovereign God who keeps His servants until their work is done.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

An English maidservant turned missionary to China, called “The Small Woman,” who led a hundred orphans over the mountains to safety.

expand to see more

GLADYS AYLWARD, an English missionary to China (1902–1970), known as “The Small Woman.”

Rejected by a mission board, she paid her own way across Siberia to reach China in 1932.

Helped run the Inn of the Eighth Happiness at Yangcheng, preaching to passing travellers.

Served as a government foot-inspector, ending foot-binding and spreading the gospel.

Led about a hundred orphaned children over the mountains to safety during the Japanese invasion.

📖 Key Scripture

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

Mat 18:5 — "And whoso shall receive one such little child in my name receiveth me."

Isa 6:8 — "Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me."

Psa 68:5 — "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Her story refutes the modern gatekeeping that measures a servant’s fitness by credentials rather than by calling and faith.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Aylward is that God chooses the weak and unqualified to confound the mighty. The boards turned her away; the Lord sent her, and through one rejected woman delivered orphans and gathered souls. Fitness for service is conferred by Christ, not by the approval of men.

Her care for the fatherless flows straight from the heart of God, the father of the fatherless. In an age that prizes self-fulfilment, Aylward spent herself for children who could repay her nothing, becoming a citizen of a foreign land for the sake of the gospel.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

A Welsh name of gladness joined to an Old English surname meaning “noble guardian.”

expand to see more

Gladys Aylward — Gladys, linked with gladness; Aylward, “noble guardian.”

Known in China by the name Ai-weh-deh, “the virtuous one.”

Title that clung to her: “The Small Woman,” for her tiny stature.

Her foot-inspector office became a roving pulpit across the villages.

Her mountain trek with the orphans became her most enduring earthly memorial.

Usage

"Gladys Aylward proved that a sovereign God needs no permission from a board to call His servant."

"Footsore and singing, the children followed Gladys Aylward over the last ridge to safety."

"When men called her unqualified, Gladys Aylward answered only to the One who sent her."
